title: From Genetic Susceptibility to Modifiable Biology: Epigenetic Plasticity, Artificial Intelligence, and Badminton as a Model of Healthy Aging
content: Genomic medicine has transformed the study of inherited susceptibility, but common chronic disease and functional aging are expressed through biological systems that remain dynamic long after the genome is established. A landmark example came in 2004, when Yang Shi and colleagues identified LSD1/KDM1A as the first histone lysine demethylase, showing that histone methylation could be enzymatically reversed. Subsequent work on histone demethylases, cancer cell state, antitumor immunity, and therapeutic reprogramming reinforced the broader principle that regulatory states can be actively remodeled. This molecular plasticity should not be confused with genetic malleability: inherited risk persists, and many biological changes are neither reversible nor clinically important. We propose a modifiable-biology framework in which disease trajectory and functional aging reflect interactions among inherited sequence, gene regulation, metabolism, nutrient status, environmental exposures, behavior, immune and endocrine signaling, and time. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help integrate longitudinal multi-omics, wearable, behavioral, exposure, and clinical data, particularly for identifying response phenotypes and prioritizing hypotheses, although causal inference still depends on study design and validation. Badminton offers a concrete human model because it combines intermittent aerobic and anaerobic effort, repeated mechanical loading, motor learning, visuospatial processing, coordination, and social engagement. High-intensity functional training (HIFT) provides a complementary model centered on strength, power, endurance, agility, and whole-body work capacity. Published studies show that both forms of complex exercise can produce measurable functional adaptation, while the molecular signatures that distinguish long-term responders remain incompletely characterized. We outline a research agenda linking chromatin biology, modifiable exposures, healthy aging, AI-enabled phenotyping, and clinically meaningful outcomes. Precision medicine, in this view, should characterize inherited constraints while testing the biology that remains measurable and changeable over time.
